messages.content: What is the central goal for predicting protein functions here?

The goal is to predict specific protein molecular functions in unseen families while distinguishing genuine functional novelty from incomplete annotations. It has two explicit performance requirements: a relative macro-AUPRC improvement of at least 10% over sequence-only transfer on family-disjoint, temporally held-out annotations, and an AUROC of at least 0.80 for distinguishing novel functions from missing annotations on independently adjudicated proteins.
What does “specific protein molecular functions” emphasize?

It emphasizes predictions about what a protein does at the molecular-function level, rather than an unspecific claim that the protein has some function. The goal calls for specificity, but it does not name particular functions or set out a required level of detail beyond that wording.
Does “unseen families” mean the performance target is about proteins outside the families represented in the comparison setting?

That is the point of the family-disjoint condition: the evaluation concerns families held apart from those used for the comparison. It makes the stated improvement a test of performance across families, not merely within the same families. The goal does not specify which families are involved.
Can you unpack the first numerical requirement without assuming a result has already been obtained?

Yes. The requirement is to achieve at least a 10% relative improvement in macro-AUPRC over sequence-only transfer, evaluated on family-disjoint, temporally held-out annotations. It is a target, not a reported result. “Relative” matters: it refers to an increase measured against the sequence-only transfer score, not an increase of ten percentage points in macro-AUPRC.
Could you give a purely illustrative calculation for that distinction?

If, purely as an arithmetic example, a sequence-only transfer baseline had a macro-AUPRC of 0.30, a 10% relative improvement would mean at least 0.33. It would not mean 0.40. Those example scores are not claims about any proteins or evaluation results here.
Why mention macro-AUPRC specifically rather than just saying prediction accuracy?

Macro-AUPRC identifies the stated measure for the function-prediction comparison. In general, AUPRC summarizes a precision–recall relationship, while “macro” indicates averaging across the prediction targets rather than treating every instance as one undifferentiated pool. The requirement is tied to that measure; it cannot be replaced by a general assertion of accuracy or by a different metric.
And what work is the temporal holdout doing in the wording?

It specifies a condition on the annotations used for evaluation: they are temporally held out. Together with the family-disjoint condition, it defines the setting in which the ≥10% relative macro-AUPRC improvement over sequence-only transfer must be assessed. The wording does not provide dates, a particular annotation source, or further details of the holdout.
The second part sounds different. What exactly must be distinguished?

It calls for distinguishing novel functions from missing annotations. Those are not interchangeable interpretations of an apparently unrecorded function: a function may be genuinely novel, or a relevant annotation may simply be incomplete. The specified target for this distinction is at least 0.80 AUROC on independently adjudicated proteins.
So a function’s absence from an annotation record is not, by itself, enough to call it novel?

Right. An absent annotation can reflect incomplete annotation rather than genuine functional novelty. That ambiguity is precisely why the goal includes a separate distinction between the two. The wording does not say that every unannotated prediction is novel, or that an unrecorded function should automatically be treated as absent.
What should I take “genuine functional novelty” to mean without reading too much into it?

Read it in contrast to incomplete annotations: the aim is to identify novelty that is not merely an artifact of a missing record. The goal does not define novelty more narrowly, such as by naming a particular biochemical mechanism, and it does not specify how novelty is established. The important stated distinction is between genuine novelty and an existing function that has not been adequately annotated.
What does the ≥0.80 AUROC threshold tell us, and what does it not tell us?

It sets a minimum AUROC for separating the novel-function and missing-annotation cases on independently adjudicated proteins. AUROC concerns how well those cases can be discriminated across decision thresholds. The number is a required performance level, not an observed score, and it does not by itself specify a particular operating threshold or the fraction of proteins in either category.
Is the AUROC requirement just another way of stating the macro-AUPRC requirement?

No. They address different parts of the goal. The ≥10% relative macro-AUPRC improvement over sequence-only transfer concerns prediction of specific molecular functions under the family-disjoint, temporal-holdout evaluation. The ≥0.80 AUROC requirement concerns distinguishing novel functions from missing annotations on independently adjudicated proteins. Meeting one metric would not, by itself, establish that the other requirement is met.
Why is independent adjudication attached to the novelty-versus-missing-annotation test?

It states the evidentiary condition for that test: the proteins used to evaluate the distinction are independently adjudicated. That matters because the two categories must be distinguishable for the AUROC target to have meaning. The goal does not describe who adjudicates them, the adjudication procedure, or its outcome.
Can I summarize the aim as generalization plus care in interpreting apparent novelty?

Yes, provided the precise requirements stay attached. The prediction goal concerns specific protein molecular functions in unseen families, with at least a 10% relative macro-AUPRC improvement over sequence-only transfer on family-disjoint, temporally held-out annotations. Alongside that, apparent novelty must be distinguished from incomplete annotation with at least 0.80 AUROC on independently adjudicated proteins. Both are goals rather than completed findings.
What approach would address both the molecular-function prediction goal and the uncertainty around apparent novelty?

A proposed approach is to combine ESM-2 embeddings with Foldseek active-site matches for GO prediction, then use assay-coverage-aware positive-unlabeled calibration to help distinguish genuine functional novelty from annotation gaps. This is a proposal for how to tackle the two parts of the goal, not a claim that either performance requirement has been met.
What are the two sources of information being combined for GO prediction?

One is ESM-2 embeddings, which provide representations derived from protein sequences. The other is Foldseek active-site matches, which bring in comparisons involving active sites. The proposal is to use both for GO prediction; it does not specify how their contributions would be weighted or combined.
Why distinguish ESM-2 embeddings from the sequence-only transfer comparison?

Because ESM-2 embeddings are themselves sequence-derived. Including them in a proposed method does not make the entire method non-sequence-based; the additional proposed ingredient is Foldseek active-site matching. The goal’s comparison remains the stated one: at least a 10% relative macro-AUPRC improvement over sequence-only transfer on family-disjoint, temporally held-out annotations. The proposal does not establish that improvement.
Does an active-site match automatically establish a protein’s GO function?

No. In this proposal, an active-site match is information to consider in GO prediction, not automatic proof of a particular function. The node does not say that every match is decisive, nor does it set a rule for what to do when an embedding-based indication and an active-site match point in different directions.
Then what does “combine” commit us to?

It commits the proposal to drawing on both ESM-2 embeddings and Foldseek active-site matches for GO prediction. It does not commit to a particular model, scoring formula, ordering of operations, or decision threshold. Those details are not specified here.
Is the novelty question answered by checking whether Foldseek finds an active-site match?

Not by that check alone. The proposal separately calls for assay-coverage-aware positive-unlabeled calibration to distinguish novelty from annotation gaps. A match or lack of one should not be equated, without further support, with either a documented function or genuine novelty.
Can you explain “positive-unlabeled” in this context?

It reflects the distinction between a function that is positively annotated and a function that is not annotated. A missing annotation leaves the protein–function relationship unlabeled for this purpose; it does not automatically establish a negative finding. That matters when trying to decide whether an apparently new function is genuinely novel or simply absent from incomplete annotations.
What does the assay-coverage-aware part add?

It says the calibration should take account of assay coverage when interpreting that uncertainty. An absent annotation may have a different evidentiary meaning depending on how much relevant assay coverage there has been. The proposal does not define a coverage measure, specify which assays count, or claim that coverage alone settles whether a function is novel.
So calibration is meant to prevent a missing label from being treated as proof of novelty?

That is a fair way to express its intended role. The proposed calibration accounts for the fact that positive annotations and unlabeled cases are not the same as confirmed positives and confirmed negatives, with assay coverage informing how to interpret the unlabeled cases. It is still a proposed way to distinguish novelty from annotation gaps, not a demonstration that every gap can be resolved.
Could you give a general illustration without implying that any particular protein has been studied?

Suppose, hypothetically, a GO function is not annotated for a protein. That absence alone does not tell us whether the function is genuinely novel for that protein or whether the annotation is missing. The proposed assay-coverage-aware positive-unlabeled calibration would take the available coverage into account when interpreting the absence. This illustration does not assign an actual label or result to any protein.
Does the proposal change what counts as the goal’s novelty assessment?

No. It suggests an approach to the same distinction: genuine functional novelty versus incomplete annotation. The stated performance target remains at least 0.80 AUROC for distinguishing novel functions from missing annotations on independently adjudicated proteins. The proposal does not report an AUROC or alter that evaluation condition.
And the GO-prediction part still has to work on unseen families?

Yes. The broader goal remains prediction of specific protein molecular functions in unseen families. Its stated comparison is the ≥10% relative macro-AUPRC improvement over sequence-only transfer on family-disjoint, temporally held-out annotations. Proposing ESM-2 embeddings plus Foldseek active-site matches identifies candidate information for GO prediction; it does not yet tell us how well that prediction generalizes.
Is assay-coverage-aware calibration itself the GO predictor, or is it doing something different?

The proposal gives them distinct roles. Combining ESM-2 embeddings and Foldseek active-site matches addresses GO prediction. Assay-coverage-aware positive-unlabeled calibration addresses how to distinguish novelty from annotation gaps. Those roles are related because the interpretation of a function prediction can be affected by incomplete annotation, but the proposal does not specify a single end-to-end architecture.
Would it be accurate to call this a sequence-and-active-site proposal with a separate safeguard against overcalling novelty?

Yes, as an informal description. More precisely, it proposes combining ESM-2 embeddings and Foldseek active-site matches for GO prediction and using assay-coverage-aware positive-unlabeled calibration to distinguish novelty from annotation gaps. Calling the calibration a safeguard describes its intended purpose, not proven effectiveness.
What should we avoid concluding from the proposal alone?

We should not conclude that a GO function has been confirmed, that a missing annotation is a true negative, or that apparent novelty has been independently established. Nor does the proposal report the ≥10% relative macro-AUPRC improvement or the ≥0.80 AUROC. It identifies an approach to those aims without supplying results or implementation details.
Can you state the proposal in one precise sentence?

Combine ESM-2 embeddings and Foldseek active-site matches for GO prediction, and use assay-coverage-aware positive-unlabeled calibration to distinguish genuine functional novelty from annotation gaps.
Can assay-coverage estimates distinguish untested GO activities from genuinely novel functions when active-site matches lack matching annotations?

That is an open question. Assay-coverage estimates might help interpret why an active-site match has no matching GO annotation, but the absence of that annotation does not by itself tell us whether the activity is untested or the function is genuinely novel. The question is whether coverage provides enough relevant information to distinguish those explanations.
What exactly is ambiguous about an active-site match without a matching annotation?

The match offers a point of comparison, while the lack of a matching annotation leaves the GO activity unresolved. The annotation could be absent because the activity has not been adequately tested or recorded; alternatively, the function under consideration might genuinely be novel. Neither interpretation follows automatically from the match or the missing annotation.
Is “untested GO activity” the same thing as an activity known not to be present?

No. “Untested” means the available testing has not established the answer. It should not be treated as a confirmed absence. That distinction is central to asking whether assay-coverage estimates can help separate an annotation gap from genuine functional novelty.
Then what could an assay-coverage estimate contribute, at least conceptually?

It could indicate how much relevant testing bears on the missing annotation. If coverage is limited, the lack of an annotation may be less informative about whether the activity exists. But an estimate would have to be relevant to the GO activity in question, and this question supplies neither coverage values nor evidence that any particular estimate can resolve the ambiguity.
Would extensive assay coverage settle it in the other direction?

Not necessarily. Even extensive coverage would need to bear on the particular activity at issue. A coverage estimate is context for interpreting missing annotations, not proof that a function is absent or genuinely novel. The question asks whether it can distinguish the cases; it does not establish that it can.
Why specify that the active-site matches lack matching annotations? Wouldn't the match alone be enough to assign the GO activity?

The missing matching annotation is what makes the interpretation difficult. An active-site match may be relevant to GO prediction, but it is not, by itself, a confirmed annotation for the activity being considered. The question focuses on whether assay-coverage estimates can clarify what that missing annotation means, rather than treating the match as a definitive assignment.
So there are two different kinds of uncertainty here?

Yes. One concerns what the active-site match implies for the GO activity. The other concerns why a matching annotation is absent. Assay-coverage estimates are being considered for the second uncertainty in particular: whether the activity may simply be untested, as opposed to the function being genuinely novel. They do not automatically eliminate the first uncertainty.
How does that relate to the proposed positive-unlabeled calibration?

It probes the proposed use of assay-coverage-aware positive-unlabeled calibration. A missing matching annotation is an unlabeled case, not an established negative. The question is whether coverage information can make that unlabeled case more interpretable when an active-site match exists but no matching GO annotation does. No calibration result is stated here.
Could we say that low coverage proves an annotation gap?

No. Low relevant coverage could make an untested activity a plausible explanation for the missing annotation, but it would not prove the activity exists or that the gap explains this particular case. The distinction being asked about requires more than treating a coverage estimate as a direct functional label.
And could we say that a missing annotation despite coverage proves genuine novelty?

No. That would also go beyond what an assay-coverage estimate establishes. Coverage may affect how informative the absence of an annotation is, but the question does not provide a basis for declaring a particular function genuinely novel.
Is this question already answered by the goal’s AUROC threshold?

No. The goal sets a target of at least 0.80 AUROC for distinguishing novel functions from missing annotations on independently adjudicated proteins. A target is not an observed result, and it does not answer whether assay-coverage estimates can make that distinction in the particular situation where active-site matches lack matching annotations.
What would count as a careful short answer to the question right now?

Assay-coverage estimates may help distinguish untested GO activities from genuinely novel functions when active-site matches lack matching annotations, but the match and the missing annotation alone do not settle the issue. Whether coverage actually makes the distinction is unresolved by the information given.
What is the hypothesis for proteins whose active-site matches are unlabeled?

The hypothesis is that, for proteins with unlabeled active-site matches, assay-coverage-aware calibration will distinguish genuine functional novelty from annotation gaps with an AUROC of at least 0.80. It is a predicted outcome, not an observed result.
How does that speak to my question about untested GO activities?

It proposes an answer for the situation you asked about: an active-site match exists, but a matching annotation is lacking. The hypothesis is that calibration informed by assay coverage can separate cases of genuine novelty from cases where an annotation is missing, reaching AUROC ≥0.80 for proteins with those unlabeled matches. Whether it actually can do so remains to be established.
What does “unlabeled active-site match” mean here? Does it mean there is no match?

No. It means there is an active-site match, but the corresponding annotation is not available for the interpretation at issue. The match itself and a matching annotation are different things; “unlabeled” should not be read as “no match” or as a confirmed absence of the GO activity.
Does an unlabeled match count as evidence of genuine novelty?

Not on its own. An unlabeled match leaves open both possibilities named in the hypothesis: genuine functional novelty and an annotation gap. The proposed calibration is meant to distinguish between them, rather than assigning novelty merely because the annotation is missing.
And what role does assay coverage play in the hypothesis?

Assay coverage is the information the calibration is proposed to account for when interpreting an unlabeled match. Conceptually, it bears on how much can be inferred from a missing annotation: an activity that has not been adequately examined should not be treated the same way as a confirmed absence. The hypothesis does not specify how coverage is estimated or used in the calibration.
Is the claim that assay coverage alone perfectly tells us which case we have?

No. The claim is about assay-coverage-aware calibration distinguishing the two cases at AUROC ≥0.80 within the specified group. It does not assert perfect separation, and it does not say that a coverage estimate by itself supplies a definitive label for any individual protein.
Why phrase the expected performance as AUROC rather than a percentage of proteins labeled correctly?

AUROC expresses how well the two categories can be discriminated across decision thresholds. The hypothesis specifies AUROC ≥0.80; it does not specify a classification threshold or a percentage correctly classified at one threshold. Describing it as, for example, “80% of proteins classified correctly” would change the claim.
Does the ≥ sign matter?

Yes. The hypothesized threshold is at least 0.80 AUROC, so 0.80 meets the stated threshold and a value below 0.80 does not. That threshold applies to distinguishing genuine novelty from annotation gaps for proteins with unlabeled active-site matches.
Is this saying all proteins with active-site matches have novel functions?

No. It concerns a distinction to be made among proteins with unlabeled active-site matches. Some cases may represent genuine novelty and others may represent annotation gaps; the hypothesis does not state how many fall into either category.
Could an annotation gap include a GO activity that simply has not been tested?

Yes, an untested activity is one possible reason a relevant annotation might be missing. But an unlabeled match does not establish that the activity is present, and the hypothesis does not assign a particular explanation to any protein. Its point is to distinguish genuine novelty from missing-annotation cases rather than conflate them.
Does this hypothesis also claim an improvement in GO prediction over sequence-only transfer?

No. Its stated outcome is AUROC ≥0.80 for the novelty-versus-annotation-gap distinction in proteins with unlabeled active-site matches. The separate goal of improving molecular-function prediction over sequence-only transfer is not a result or an additional performance claim made by this hypothesis.
Are we claiming the proposed calibration has already reached that AUROC?
No. “Will distinguish” states the expectation being hypothesized. There is no reported AUROC measurement here, so it would be inaccurate to say the threshold has already been reached.
What is the exact scope of the AUROC claim?

It is scoped to proteins with unlabeled active-site matches, and the discrimination is between genuine functional novelty and annotation gaps. The hypothesis does not say the same AUROC would hold for every protein, for matches with available annotations, or for GO prediction considered as a whole.
If I rephrase it as “missing annotations are negatives, and calibration finds the positives,” have I kept the meaning?

Not quite. A missing annotation should not be treated as a confirmed negative; that uncertainty is precisely why the distinction matters. A faithful rephrasing is that assay-coverage-aware calibration is hypothesized to distinguish genuine novelty from annotation gaps among proteins with unlabeled active-site matches, at AUROC ≥0.80.
Does “genuine novelty” mean simply that no matching GO annotation appears beside an active-site match?

No. That observation describes an unlabeled match, not a settled conclusion about novelty. The hypothesis asks whether calibration can distinguish genuine novelty from the alternative explanation of an annotation gap within that ambiguous set.
Can you state the hypothesis without making it sound like a demonstrated finding?
We hypothesize that assay-coverage-aware calibration will achieve AUROC ≥0.80 when distinguishing genuine functional novelty from annotation gaps in proteins with unlabeled active-site matches.
How would we evaluate the assay-coverage-aware calibration hypothesis?

The planned activity is to compare novelty-versus-annotation-gap AUROC with assay-coverage calibration against AUROC without calibration, using 400 independently adjudicated proteins with unlabeled Foldseek active-site matches. This describes a comparison to perform, not an experiment that has already produced results.
Which proteins are included in that comparison?

The specified set consists of 400 independently adjudicated proteins with unlabeled Foldseek active-site matches. The number 400 is the total stated for the activity; it is not stated as 400 proteins in each novelty-or-gap category.
Does “unlabeled Foldseek active-site matches” mean Foldseek found nothing for those proteins?

No. These proteins have Foldseek active-site matches. “Unlabeled” means the matches lack the matching annotations relevant to the novelty-versus-gap question. An unlabeled match is not the same as no match, and it does not by itself establish either genuine novelty or an annotation gap.
Why does the activity specify independently adjudicated proteins if the matches are unlabeled?

Those descriptions serve different purposes. The active-site matches are unlabeled in the sense that matching annotations are lacking. Independent adjudication provides the basis for evaluating whether the cases represent genuine novelty or annotation gaps. The activity does not say who performs that adjudication or how it is carried out.
What exactly is being compared across the calibrated and uncalibrated conditions?

The comparison is between their AUROC values for distinguishing novelty from annotation gaps on the specified 400 proteins. It is not a comparison of GO-prediction macro-AUPRC, nor is the uncalibrated condition the sequence-only transfer baseline from the broader prediction goal.
Does “assay-coverage-calibrated” specify how coverage is estimated?

No. It identifies the condition that uses assay-coverage calibration, but this activity does not give a coverage measure, calibration formula, or list of assays. Those details should not be inferred from the comparison as stated.
Then what can we safely say about the uncalibrated side?

It is the uncalibrated comparator for the same novelty-versus-gap AUROC question. The activity does not supply an implementation or a score for it. Its role here is to make the value of the assay-coverage-calibrated condition assessable by comparison, rather than considering that condition’s AUROC in isolation.
Is the activity asking us to compare individual protein labels, or a discrimination metric?

It specifically calls for comparing AUROC, a discrimination metric, between the two conditions. Independently adjudicated cases make that comparison meaningful, but the activity does not set out an individual-protein decision rule or claim that every protein will be classified correctly.
How does this comparison bear on the hypothesis of AUROC ≥0.80?

The calibrated AUROC would address the hypothesis’s proposed threshold for distinguishing genuine novelty from annotation gaps in proteins with unlabeled active-site matches. Comparing it with the uncalibrated AUROC also asks whether calibration makes a difference on that metric. Neither AUROC is reported here, so the activity does not tell us whether the threshold is reached or whether calibration improves discrimination.
Could a comparison favor calibration even if its AUROC were below 0.80?

Conceptually, yes: one condition could have a higher AUROC than another without reaching 0.80. That is why the comparison between calibrated and uncalibrated AUROC and the hypothesis’s ≥0.80 threshold are distinct questions. This activity supplies no values for either condition.
And reaching 0.80 would not, by itself, tell us how the uncalibrated condition performed?

Correct. A calibrated AUROC considered alone would not give the difference between the two conditions. The planned activity explicitly compares the assay-coverage-calibrated and uncalibrated AUROCs on the specified proteins.
What does the temporal holdout from the GO-prediction goal contribute to this particular activity?

This activity does not specify a temporal holdout. It specifies 400 independently adjudicated proteins with unlabeled Foldseek active-site matches and a calibrated-versus-uncalibrated novelty-versus-gap AUROC comparison. The family-disjoint, temporally held-out macro-AUPRC comparison belongs to the broader GO-prediction goal, not to an evaluation condition stated here.
Should we describe the 400 proteins as a random sample or as evenly divided between novelty and gaps?

No. Neither the sampling method nor the numbers in the two categories are stated. The precise description available is 400 independently adjudicated proteins with unlabeled Foldseek active-site matches.
If the active-site matches lack matching annotations, is the comparison treating those absent annotations as confirmed negatives?

No. The comparison is designed around distinguishing genuine novelty from annotation gaps precisely because an absent matching annotation is ambiguous. Independent adjudication supplies the evaluation basis; the unlabeled match itself should not be converted into a confirmed negative.
What would a higher calibrated AUROC mean, if the comparison eventually found one?

It would mean the calibrated condition showed better discrimination between novelty and annotation gaps than the uncalibrated condition by AUROC on those 400 independently adjudicated proteins. That is a conditional interpretation, not a reported finding. The activity alone would not specify why a difference arose or establish performance outside the stated set.
Does this activity also test whether ESM-2 embeddings plus Foldseek matches improve GO prediction?

Not directly. Its stated outcome is novelty-versus-gap AUROC under assay-coverage-calibrated and uncalibrated conditions. Although Foldseek active-site matches define the proteins included, this activity does not compare GO-prediction macro-AUPRC or test the proposed combination with ESM-2 embeddings.
Can you state the activity precisely without implying its outcome?

On 400 independently adjudicated proteins with unlabeled Foldseek active-site matches, compare assay-coverage-calibrated versus uncalibrated AUROC for distinguishing genuine novelty from annotation gaps.
What did the calibrated-versus-uncalibrated comparison show?
Across 400 independently adjudicated proteins with unlabeled active-site matches, assay-coverage calibration raised novelty-versus-annotation-gap AUROC from 0.72 to 0.84.
Which score belongs to which condition?

The uncalibrated novelty-versus-gap AUROC was 0.72. With assay-coverage calibration, it was 0.84. Both figures refer to the comparison across the 400 independently adjudicated proteins with unlabeled active-site matches.
How large is the difference between those AUROC values?
The difference is 0.12 AUROC units: 0.84 minus 0.72. That is a difference in a discrimination metric, not a statement that 12% more individual proteins were classified correctly.
What does a higher novelty-versus-gap AUROC mean here?

It means the calibrated condition showed better discrimination between genuine novelty and annotation gaps across decision thresholds on this evaluated set. AUROC does not, by itself, give the number of correctly classified proteins at any one threshold.
Were these just proteins without active-site matches?
No. The 400 proteins had active-site matches that were unlabeled. The lack of a matching annotation is the ambiguity at issue; it does not mean no active-site match was found.
Does “unlabeled” mean those proteins were judged to have no relevant function?

No. An unlabeled match is not a confirmed negative. The reported AUROC concerns distinguishing genuine novelty from annotation gaps, so treating every missing annotation as an established absence would erase the distinction being evaluated.
How can the proteins be independently adjudicated and still have unlabeled matches?

Those terms describe different aspects of the comparison. The active-site matches lack matching annotations, while the proteins were independently adjudicated for evaluating the novelty-versus-gap distinction. The evidence does not give further details of the adjudication process.
Does the result say how many of the 400 proteins were genuine novelty cases?
No. It gives the total number of independently adjudicated proteins and the two AUROC values, but not the number assigned to either category.
Can we tell from these numbers which individual proteins were correctly identified?

No. The reported result is an aggregate AUROC comparison. It does not provide individual predictions, adjudicated labels, or a decision threshold for assigning either category to a particular protein.
Is this evidence about GO-prediction performance in general?

It is evidence about novelty-versus-gap discrimination for the specified 400 proteins with unlabeled active-site matches. It does not report GO-prediction macro-AUPRC or a comparison against sequence-only transfer.
Does the change from 0.72 to 0.84 show which aspect of assay coverage was responsible?

No. The result attributes the higher reported AUROC to the assay-coverage-calibrated condition in this comparison, but it does not specify a coverage measure or isolate which aspect of the calibration accounts for the difference.
Could I describe 0.84 as an accuracy of 84%?
No. The reported value is AUROC, not classification accuracy. Saying “84% accuracy” would substitute a different metric and imply an operating threshold that is not given.
Do we know whether the 0.12 difference is statistically significant?
That is not stated. The evidence reports the set of 400 proteins and the increase in AUROC from 0.72 to 0.84, but gives no uncertainty interval or significance test.
What is the narrowest faithful conclusion from the result?

On 400 independently adjudicated proteins with unlabeled active-site matches, the assay-coverage-calibrated condition had a higher novelty-versus-gap AUROC than the uncalibrated condition: 0.84 versus 0.72. The result does not establish how either condition would perform outside that stated comparison.
What is the decision about assay-coverage calibration?
Retain assay-coverage calibration for novelty triage. The stated reason is that adjudicated novelty-versus-gap AUROC reached 0.84, exceeding the 0.80 target.
What does “novelty triage” mean in this decision?

It refers to distinguishing cases of genuine functional novelty from cases where an annotation is missing. Retaining calibration means continuing to use assay-coverage information for that distinction; the decision does not specify a particular triage workflow or an individual-protein decision rule.
Why does the 0.84 figure justify retaining it?
The decision explicitly ties retention to the adjudicated AUROC of 0.84. That value exceeds the stated 0.80 target for novelty-versus-gap discrimination by 0.04 AUROC units.
Is 0.84 an accuracy of 84%?

No. It is AUROC, which measures discrimination across decision thresholds. The decision does not report classification accuracy at a chosen threshold or say that 84% of proteins received the correct individual label.
Does exceeding the target mean every apparent novel function can be identified reliably?

No. The decision is based on an aggregate adjudicated AUROC. Exceeding 0.80 supports retaining calibration for novelty triage, but it does not guarantee a correct interpretation for every protein or eliminate the ambiguity of every missing annotation.
Does retaining calibration mean treating proteins without matching annotations as genuinely novel?

No. The purpose of novelty triage is to distinguish genuine novelty from annotation gaps, not to equate a missing annotation with novelty. Retaining assay-coverage calibration preserves that distinction.
Is this a decision about the GO predictor as a whole?

Its stated scope is assay-coverage calibration for novelty triage. It does not decide how to combine ESM-2 embeddings and Foldseek active-site matches for GO prediction, and the 0.84 AUROC is not a reported macro-AUPRC improvement over sequence-only transfer.
Does the decision specify a new AUROC target?
No. It uses the 0.80 target as the benchmark and notes that the adjudicated AUROC reached 0.84. Retaining calibration does not change the target or establish a new one.
Should I describe the margin as four percentage points?

It is clearer to say the AUROC exceeded the target by 0.04 AUROC units: 0.84 versus 0.80. Calling it a four-percentage-point increase in classification accuracy would be misleading, because accuracy is not the metric reported.
Does “retain” tell us how assay coverage is calculated?

No. It states a decision to keep assay-coverage calibration in novelty triage, together with the performance reason for that decision. It does not specify a coverage estimate, calibration formula, or operational threshold.
Can we say the decision establishes performance for proteins beyond those adjudicated?
No. The stated reason is the adjudicated AUROC reaching 0.84. The decision does not provide a separate result for other proteins or guarantee the same AUROC in another setting.
What is the most precise one-sentence statement of the decision?
Retain assay-coverage calibration for novelty triage because adjudicated novelty-versus-gap AUROC reached 0.84, exceeding the 0.80 target.
What is the plan for the next comparison?

Retain assay-coverage calibration, train through 2024, and then compare Foldseek–ESM-2 with sequence-only transfer using macro-AUPRC on Pfam-disjoint 2025–2026 GO annotations. This is a planned comparison, not a reported result.
What does “train through 2024” mean relative to the GO annotations used for comparison?

It sets the training period through 2024, with the comparison conducted on GO annotations from 2025–2026. The plan does not give a more precise date within 2024 or specify a finer schedule for either year of evaluation annotations.
Why specify both a time period and Pfam-disjoint annotations?

They describe different conditions of the comparison. The 2025–2026 annotations provide the temporal separation from training through 2024. “Pfam-disjoint” specifies separation by Pfam families. Having a later annotation period alone would not express the family-disjoint condition, and family disjointness alone would not express the temporal condition.
Does Pfam-disjoint simply mean the evaluation is on unseen families?

It expresses the family-separation aspect of that aim using Pfam. The plan does not name the families, state how many are involved, or provide a detailed rule for handling every possible family assignment. The important condition stated here is that the 2025–2026 GO annotation comparison is Pfam-disjoint.
